blocks.text: So he writes. However plausible this may be, it does not persuade me at all, because I see that the ancient interpreters of Sacred Scripture, with almost unanimous agreement, interpret בת־יענה as ostrich. Since this very point is in question, I now undertake to prove it. To begin with the most ancient, the LXX translators mostly render it στρουθὸν [strouthon] or στρουθίον [strouthion], that is, ostrich. Thus in the very passage we are dealing with, Levit. XI, 16., they have τὸν στρουθὸν [ton strouthon] ^{(2)}. And at Iob. XXX, 29. ἑταῖρος (γέγονα) στρουθῶν [hetairos (gegona) strouthōn]. And at Esa. XXXIV, 13. αὐλὴ στρουθῶν [aulē strouthōn]. And at Esa. XLIII, 20. εὐλογήσει με, etc. θυγατέρες στρουθῶν [eulogēsei me, etc. thygateres strouthōn]. And at Thren. IV, 3. ὡς στρουθίον ἐν ἐρήμῳ [hōs strouthion en erēmō]. [col. 221] You will say that the word is ambiguous, because στρουθὸς [strouthos] is sometimes taken for the sparrow, one of the small birds, and sometimes for the ostrich, or, what is the same, for the strutho-camelus, which in Latin is also called passer marinus [sea sparrow] in Plautus, Ausonius, Festus and others; and that it can be doubted in which sense those interpreters used it. So it is; but almost all the ancients take it of ostriches. Chrysostom on Job: Στρουθοὺς λέγει τοὺς στρουθοκαμήλους, ὡς καὶ Σύμμαχος ἐξέδωκεν [Strouthous legei tous strouthokamēlous, hōs kai Symmachos exedōken]. So too Eusebius, Basil, Jerome, Theodoret and Procopius on Isaiah, Olympiodorus on Jeremiah, and most recently Suidas under Σειρῆνας [Seirēnas]: Στρουθὸν λέγει, ὃν ἡμεῖς στρουθοκάμηλον λέγομεν [Strouthon legei, hon hēmeis strouthokamēlon legomen]. Nor did Aquila, Symmachus, Theodotion and the Vulgate translator think otherwise: the last consistently renders struthiones [ostriches], the others στρουθοκαμήλους [strouthokamēlous]. Finally, alone among the ancients, as far as I remember, Novatian takes it of the sparrow, in the book On Jewish Foods, chapter 3: When he forbids the sparrow, he says, he rebukes intemperance. And alone among the moderns Fuller embraces the same view, [II, 816] relying, that is, on this rule, which he pronounces as if from the tripod: The noun στρουθὸς [strouthos], placed alone and by itself, with no epithet added to mark a distinction, means sparrow in Latin. No doubt the learned man, who is incredibly precise in such matters, had read that the ostrich is called στρουθὸν κατάγαιον [strouthon katagaion] by Herodotus; μέγαν [megan] by Aristophanes, Xenophon, Athenaeus and Strato in the Anthology; Λιβυκόν [Libykon] by Aristotle; Ἀράβιον [Arabion] by Heraclides; χαμαιπετῆ [chamaipetē] by Lucian; χερσαῖον [chersaion] by Aelian; στρουθὸν τῶν ἀπτήνων [strouthon tōn aptēnōn] by Pausanias; Μαυρούσιον [Maurousion] by Herodian; ἄγριον [agrion] by Hesychius. So he thought that what usually happens always happens. It is certain, however, that στρουθὸν [strouthon] is not rarely taken for the ostrich even without an epithet. For who would say that sparrows' feathers, not ostriches', are meant by Theophrastus when he says that helmets are adorned τῶν στρουθῶν πτεροῖς [tōn strouthōn pterois], History of Plants, book 4, chapter 5? And in the chapter just before, when he writes that in the part of Libya where it does not rain there are born πτῶκα, καὶ δορκάδα, καὶ στρουθὸν, καὶ ἕτερα τῶν θηρίων [ptōka, kai dorkada, kai strouthon, kai hetera tōn thēriōn], the hare, and the roe, and the struthus (as the translator, often inept, has it there) and other wild beasts: what else can στρουθὸς [strouthos] be there than the ostrich, which many count among wild beasts because it is of a nature intermediate between birds and beasts? And the στρουθῶν συνωρίδας ὀκτὼ [strouthōn synōridas oktō] which, as Callixenus of Rhodes relates ^{a)}, went forth in the procession of Ptolemy: who would think they were pairs of sparrows rather than of ostriches, as in the chariot of Venus? And would the most learned Scholiast mean a sparrow's foot when he says that Cleocritus is mocked by Aristophanes in the Birds ὡς στρουθόποδα, τουτέστι μεγαλόπουν [hōs strouthopoda, toutesti megalopoun]? And did Pollux speak of sparrow skins in the passage where he relates ^{b)} that the Arabs covered themselves in war στρουθῶν δοραῖς [strouthōn dorais] instead of shields and breastplates; or Strabo, when he writes ^{c)} that the Struthophagi hunt these birds ταῖς δοραῖς τῶν στρουθῶν σκεπασθέντας [tais dorais tōn strouthōn skepasthentas], so that, deceived by this appearance, the birds approach more incautiously? And among the Ethiopian animals that Apollonius saw, when Philostratus names together ἔλαφοι, καὶ δορκάδες, καὶ στρουθοὶ, καὶ ὄνοι [elaphoi, kai dorkades, kai strouthoi, kai onoi], who would understand sparrows by the name στρουθῶν [strouthōn], and believe they are reckoned with deer, roes and wild asses among the wild beasts of Ethiopia? These examples, then, if I am not mistaken, amply show that no trust is to be placed in Fuller's rule mentioned above, and that what I said is perfectly true: στρουθὸν [strouthon], even taken by itself, is said of the ostrich as well as of the sparrow. That this was familiar even to the Attic writers is attested by Hesychius in these words: Στρουθός· ὁ καταφερὴς, καὶ λάγνος. Ἀττικοὶ δὲ τὰς στρουθοκαμήλους [Strouthos; ho katapherēs, kai lagnos. Attikoi de tas strouthokamēlous]. So that even speaking in Attic fashion the LXX translators could use it thus. If you ask why they did not rather use the name struthocamelus, or at least some epithet to avoid the ambiguity of the word, the answer is ready. For in the age in which they lived the name struthocamelus was not yet in use; I do not know whether anyone uses it before Strabo, except that Diodorus, a few years older, seems [II, 817] to indicate it when he relates in book 3 that among the Struthophagi there is a kind of bird μεμιγμένην ἔχων τὴν φύσιν, τῷ χερσαίῳ ζώῳ, δι᾽ ἣν τῆς συνθέτου τετύχηκε [col. 222] προσηγορίας [memigmenēn echōn tēn physin, tō chersaiō zōō, di᾽ hēn tēs synthetou tetychēke prosēgorias], which has a nature mixed with a land animal, and has therefore obtained a compound name. Hence it is that Galen, so many centuries later than the Greek translators, hardly dares to use the name struthiocamelus without a preface, as new and unknown to the ancients. Thus in book 3 of On Foods, chapter 20, he says: Τὸ μὲν τῶν χηνῶν ὄνομα σύνεθές ἐστι καὶ τοῖς παλαιοῖς· τὸ δὲ τῶν στρουθοκαμήλων ἄηθες. ὀνομάζουσι γὰρ αὐτὰς μεγάλας στρουθούς [To men tōn chēnōn onoma synethes esti kai tois palaiois; to de tōn strouthokamēlōn aēthes. onomazousi gar autas megalas strouthous]. The name of geese was indeed customary even among the ancients, but that of struthocameli is unusual; for they call them great sparrows. And in the book De prob. suc. alim., chapter 6: Ἐν δὲ τοῖς μεγάλοις στρουθοῖς, ἃς νῦν ὀνομάζουσι στρουθοκαμήλους [En de tois megalois strouthois, has nyn onomazousi strouthokamēlous]; In the great sparrows, which they now call struthocameli. But they preferred to say simply στρουθοὺς [strouthous] rather than στρουθοὺς μεγάλους [strouthous megalous] or καταγαίους [katagaious], etc., both because the Hebrew בת יענה bath jaana has no epithet attached, and because there was no need to add anything, since the matter itself shows that this word in the Prophets describes birds which have nothing in common with sparrows except the bare name: birds, I say, that are solitary and dwell in desert and dreadful places; whereas sparrows fly in flocks and more willingly frequent cultivated and fruitful places.
